name: ACID vs BASE
intent: Two ways to think about data guarantees: strict all-or-nothing transactions (ACID), or looser, highly available updates that settle over time (BASE).
scenario: A bank transfer moves $100 from account A to account B. In a different part of the same product, millions of users are liking posts at the same time.
problem: Real operations are made of several steps, and machines crash and run concurrently. A transfer that debits A and then crashes before crediting B loses money. Two simultaneous withdrawals can both succeed against the same balance. On the other hand, forcing every operation to be perfectly strict is slow and limits how far a system can scale or stay available.

howItWorks.title: Atomicity: all or nothing
howItWorks.text: A transaction's steps either all take effect or none do. If the process crashes after the debit but before the credit, the database rolls the debit back, so the money never vanishes.

howItWorks.title: Consistency: rules always hold
howItWorks.text: A transaction moves the database from one valid state to another. Constraints such as 'total money is conserved' or 'balance is not negative' are checked, and a transaction that would break them is rejected.

howItWorks.title: Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere
howItWorks.text: Even when two transactions run at the same time, the result is as if they ran one after the other. Locking or versioning stops two withdrawals from both reading the same starting balance.

howItWorks.title: Durability: committed means saved
howItWorks.text: Once a transaction commits, its changes survive crashes and power loss, because they are written to a log on disk before the commit is acknowledged.

howItWorks.title: BASE: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent
howItWorks.text: Many large distributed stores relax those guarantees to scale and stay up. They accept writes on any node (basically available), let state change as replicas catch up (soft state), and promise that, if updates stop, all copies will converge (eventual consistency).

pros: ACID: correctness is the database's job, so application code stays simpler
ACID: safe for money, orders, inventory and anything where mistakes are costly
BASE: scales out easily and stays available through failures
BASE: low latency, because writes need no global coordination
cons: ACID: coordination and locking limit throughput and are hard across many machines
ACID: a failure or partition can make the system refuse work
BASE: reads can be stale and concurrent updates can conflict
BASE: the application must cope with temporary inconsistency and resolve conflicts
whenToUse: Use ACID for payments, bookings, stock levels, accounts and any invariant that must never break
Use BASE-style stores for feeds, likes, counters, carts, sessions and analytics
Mix them: transactional database for money, eventually consistent store for the timeline
whenNotToUse: Do not use eventual consistency where a stale read causes real harm, such as double-spending
Do not pay for strict transactions on data where being slightly out of date is harmless
Do not assume 'NoSQL' means BASE or 'SQL' means ACID: both ends are configurable
pitfalls: Holding transactions open for a long time and blocking everyone else
Choosing a weak isolation level and getting subtle anomalies under concurrency
Treating eventual consistency as 'consistent soon enough' without handling conflicts
Sprinkling multi-step updates across services with no transaction at all
